You have a constitutional right to not incriminate yourself or testify against yourself, that's about it. You do not have a right to not provide to authorities evidence that pertains to a legal investigation.

Now, when the NSA collects data on everyone in general before any specific crime has been committed, that is one thing. There are great arguments that such spying goes beyond powers appointed by the constitution and violates due process, etc. But in the case of the San Bernardino murders, a serious crime has been committed and law enforcement has reason to believe that evidence related to the case is encrypted on the iPhone used by the murderers. Right now, encryption produced by Apple is supposedly obstructing the investigation. If the FBI really does need Apple to unlock the phone, then Apple will have to unlock the phone.

Concerns that US or Russian or Chinese intel may want to build backdoors into all phones are indeed justified. But those concerns are ultimately irrelevant to the matter at hand. If Apple produced magical safes that for whatever reason the FBI couldn't break into, and evidence pertaining to a criminal case was hidden within such a safe, then the FBI would be well within its powers to get the courts to compel Apple to unlock the safe. That the evidence is encrypted on a phone's drive rather than locked inside a magical safe is irrelevant to the courts and law enforcement.

It is important that law enforcement be able to access evidence to investigate and prosecute actual criminal cases. It is also important that law enforcement doesn't collect data on everyone before people have actually committed crimes. But concerns that the former might lead to the latter do not invalidate the former. Apple will have to unlock the phone, there's no way around it. And it will be up to Apple to release some sort of update to ensure that other phones aren't susceptible to possible privacy violations as a consequence.

Ultimately it is up to the people to not use any form of technology for anything they want to never be made public.
